# How Long Is a Coastline? {#sec-coastline}

Ask how long the British coastline is, and you will get an answer. The answer will be a number of
kilometres. It will come from an atlas, or from a database maintained by a government agency, and
it will carry three or four significant figures.

The number is not wrong. It is worse than wrong. It measures nothing. It is a measurement of a quantity that does not
exist, and the fact that the measurement can be performed, reported, and believed is the subject
of this chapter.

The paper that established this is three pages long. It appeared in *Science* on 5 May 1967, under
the title "How Long Is the Coast of Britain? Statistical Self-Similarity and Fractional
Dimension," and it has been cited 4,100 times according to OpenAlex [@mandelbrot1967].

Three pages, one question, and an answer that changes what a length measurement means. What I want
to do in this chapter is not summarise it — the summary is one sentence — but follow the
machinery, because the machinery is the part that transferred to other subjects, and it is the
part that is still misused fifty years later.

## The experiment you can run in ten minutes

Take a map. Take a pair of dividers, the kind used in navigation, set to a fixed opening. Walk
them along the coastline, counting steps, all the way around. Multiply the number of steps by the
opening. That is your measurement of the length.

Now halve the opening and do it again.

The measured length increases. It has to. It has to: with a smaller opening you can follow inlets and
promontories that the larger opening cut across. Halve it again, and the length increases again.

This is not an error. It does not converge. Every reduction in the ruler reveals a finer
layer of structure that must be traversed. The coastline is rough at every scale you can look at,
because the processes that made it — erosion, deposition, faulting — do not have a characteristic
length scale. There is no "true" coastline underneath the approximations.

So the question has no answer. Not because measurement is hard. The reason is that the quantity presupposes something false: that length is a property
of the object rather than of the object and the instrument together.

I ran this experiment once with a photocopied map and a pair of compasses, and what struck me was
not the divergence but how quickly it appears. Two doublings of the ruler gave a difference of
about a third. The claim that a coastline has a length is not approximately true and slowly
degrading; it is false at the resolution of an ordinary atlas.

## Why a coastline, and not a mountain range

The choice of demonstration object is a rhetorical decision, and Mandelbrot's choice was better than
it looks.

A coastline has four properties that make it an unusually effective vehicle for a mathematical
idea.

**It is familiar.** Everyone has seen a coastline on a map. The puzzle does not require the reader
to accept an exotic dataset.

**It is measurable by a procedure anyone can reproduce.** Dividers and a map. No instruments, no
statistical training, no access to a laboratory.

**The measurement has a well-established official answer.** Atlases publish coastline lengths.
That gives the argument a target: not an abstract claim about undefined quantities, but a specific
number in a specific reference work that turns out to be an artefact of an unstated convention.

**The alternative exists and is not exotic.** Richardson had already produced the power law. The
piece is therefore a reinterpretation rather than a discovery, which lowers the burden of
persuasion: the reader is asked to accept a new reading of an old table, not a new world.

I have come to think that the third property does most of the work. **An argument is strongest when
it takes a number that the reader already trusts and shows what the number depends on.** That is
also the fastest way to make an enemy, which is why the rest of this book's material contains so
many papers that were ignored for a decade.

## Richardson, and the appendix nobody read

The observation is older than the paper, and the story of how it was ignored is instructive far
beyond geography.

The person who noticed was Lewis Fry Richardson, a British physicist turned meteorologist, who
spent the last part of his career applying mathematical methods to the study of war. The appendix
to his book on deadly quarrels contains a table of border lengths measured at different scales,
and a fitted relationship between measured length and ruler size. The appendix is titled "The
Problem of Contiguity" and was published in the *General Systems Yearbook* in 1961
[@richardson1961].

Richardson had died in 1958. The paper appeared three years later. He never saw it in print.

Mandelbrot cited it as reference number two, and added a remark that has become famous among
people who like this story: the relationship was entirely empirical, proposed by Richardson, and
unfortunately attracted no attention.

Three reasons suggest themselves for the neglect, and all of them are structural rather than
personal.

**It appeared in the wrong place.** A multidisciplinary yearbook, read by systems theorists, is
not where geographers or statisticians look.

**It had no theory attached.** A power law fitted to border lengths does not obviously belong to
any discipline's problem set. Geographers did not consider measurement error a geographic
question. Statisticians saw no general significance in an exponent describing maps.

**Its author was gone.** Nobody was left to promote it, respond to objections, or apply it
elsewhere.

I mention the reasons because they are not specific to 1961. A correct empirical regularity with
no owner will sit unread for a decade, and what rescues it is usually not more data but an
interpretation that makes it belong somewhere.

## Three ways for a number to fail

Before following Mandelbrot's solution, it is worth separating this problem from two others it is
usually confused with. The distinction is the book's, and it does real work in later chapters.

**Failure by noise.** The quantity exists, and your estimate of it is imprecise. Remedy: more data,
better estimators, honest intervals.

**Failure by undefinedness.** The quantity does not exist because the question is malformed.
Coastline length is the example here, and so is the question "what is the average size of a number
I am thinking of" — not because the answer is hard but because there is nothing to answer about.
Remedy: change the question.

**Failure by non-existence.** The quantity is well defined, and its defining expression diverges.
The variance of a stable distribution with exponent below two is the example from Chapter 1.
Remedy: change the question, or change the statistic.

Three failures, three different remedies, and the diagnosis determines the remedy. The reason to
insist on the distinction is that all three present identically in practice: somebody computes
something, and the number will not settle down.

When a number will not settle, the reflex is to look for more data. This is the correct response
to the first failure and a waste of a career in the other two. **Before enlarging the sample, find
out which failure you are facing.**

## Richardson's other problem

It is worth knowing what Richardson was actually doing, because it explains why a table of border
lengths ended up in the appendix of a book about war.

His subject was the mathematics of conflict. He wanted to know whether the frequency and severity
of wars obeyed any regular pattern, and to answer that he needed to measure things that are
notoriously hard to measure: how long borders are, how many pairs of countries are in contact,
which countries count as neighbours. **The scale-dependence of a border measurement was, for him, a
nuisance standing between him and a question about war.**

That is the ordinary origin of most useful quantitative ideas. Someone is trying to answer
something else, runs into a measurement that will not behave, records the anomaly, and moves on.

Richardson also illustrates a second point that recurs in this book. He was working outside the
discipline that owned his subject matter — a physicist and meteorologist writing about war — and
the work was published after he died. **Anomalies recorded by outsiders, posthumously, in
interdisciplinary venues, are the least likely kind of finding to be picked up.** The wonder is
not that his observation sat for six years; it is that it was found at all.

## The replacement: measure roughness instead

Mandelbrot's move was to stop asking for a length and start asking how the measured length behaves
as the ruler shrinks.

Write the ruler opening as G and the measured length as L(G). The empirical regularity Richardson
had found, and that Mandelbrot reinterpreted, is that L(G) falls as G rises, according to a power
law:

[F] L(G) ≈ M · G^(1−D)

The exponent contains a new parameter, D, and the claim of the paper is that D is not a fitting
constant but a geometric property of the curve: its dimension.

The argument for that claim runs through a family of curves that can be counted exactly. The Koch
curve is the standard example. Start with a line segment. Divide it into three equal parts,
remove the middle one, and replace it with two sides of an equilateral triangle. Each segment
becomes four segments, each one third as long. Repeat.

Count the self-similar pieces. The whole curve is made of four copies of itself, each scaled by a
factor of one third. Define

[F] D = − log N / log r

with N the number of copies and r the scale factor. For the Koch curve, N = 4, r = 1/3, so
D = log 4 / log 3 ≈ 1.262.

Nothing about that calculation involves estimation. N is an integer you can count and r is one
third by construction. The dimension of the Koch curve is not measured; it is derived. The value
of such curves, in this argument, is that they are **standard parts**: objects whose dimension is
known exactly, against which any estimation procedure can be calibrated.

That is why the next step works. The standard parts pay for themselves. Plot the measured lengths against the ruler openings on
logarithmic axes. For a strictly self-similar curve the points fall on a line whose slope is
1 − D. For a natural coastline, Mandelbrot argued, the points fall approximately on a line, and
the same interpretation applies.

Notice what has been gained and what has been given up. Given up: the length of the coastline,
which never existed. Gained: a quantity that does exist, can be estimated, and — this is the
substantive claim — describes something real about the object's geometry.

![The same construction at three resolutions. Each refinement multiplies the number of segments by four and reduces their length by a third, so the measured length grows without bound while the curve stays inside a bounded region. Drawn for this book from the construction rule.](../../figures/fig02-koch-refinement.png){#fig-koch}

## The six numbers, and how to read them

The paper reports six dimensions, on page 637. I list them with the paper's own descriptions,
because the descriptions matter as much as the numbers.

| Object | D reported |
| --- | --- |
| A straight frontier (limiting case) | 1.00 |
| The west coast of Britain | 1.25 |
| The land frontier of Germany, about 1899 | 1.15 |
| The land frontier between Spain and Portugal | 1.14 |
| The coast of Australia | 1.13 |
| The coast of South Africa | 1.02 |

Two things about this table require comment, and both are about method rather than about
geography.

**First, these are Mandelbrot's reinterpretation of Richardson's data, not measurements made for
the paper.** The text is explicit about this: he proposes to interpret the data as implying, for
example, that the dimension of the west coast of Great Britain is 1.25.

**Second, two of the cases were selected by eye.** The paper says that the west coast of Britain
was chosen because it looks like one of the most irregular in the world, and that South Africa was
chosen because it looks like one of the smoothest in the atlas. This is exploration, not sampling.
It is fine for building an intuition — the ordering of the numbers does match the visual
impression — and it cannot support a statistical inference.

The range is what makes the quantity useful. Narrow it and the measure dies. If every coastline came out near
1.2, the measure would carry no information. Because the extremes sit at 1.02 and 1.25, the
measure discriminates, and the ordering matches the eye.

A widely circulated seventh value does not appear in the paper. Several secondary sources — Chinese
and English alike — give the dimension of a circle as 1.15. It does not appear in Mandelbrot
(1967). The paper's Figure 1 caption states only that for a circle the measured length converges to
a limit as the step size goes to zero, which is the thin-tailed case. The number appears in the
secondary literature and not in the original, and this book records it as a verified absence
rather than repeating it.

## Three ways dimension gets used, and one of them is dangerous

Dimension is a good example of a tool that was adopted faster than it was understood. Three
usages are distinguishable, and it is worth separating them because they carry different risks.

**As a descriptive index.** "This surface has a higher fractal dimension than that one." The claim
is comparative and local, and it needs only that the measurement procedure be held fixed. This
usage is safe, and it is the majority of the applied literature.

**As a diagnostic.** A change in measured dimension signals a change in regime: a material
fractures, a tissue becomes diseased, a market changes character. This usage requires the
measurement to be stable enough that a change in the number reflects a change in the object,
rather than a change in the analyst. Usually it is, if the procedure is fixed in advance.

**As an input to a model.** The estimated dimension is fed into a formula that predicts something
else. **This is the dangerous usage**, because it propagates the estimate's uncertainty into a
quantity that may be far more sensitive to it — and the uncertainty of a dimension estimate is
large enough, as the estimation literature shows, that the propagated error swamps most model
predictions.

The distinction is not aesthetic. It is the difference between using a ruler to compare two
things and using it to calculate a load-bearing number.

## How stable is a dimension?

Here the story takes the shape it keeps for the rest of Part I. The tool works. The number moves.

Estimating a dimension or an exponent from data is a problem with an unusually bad reputation, and
the reputation is earned. Taqqu, Teverovsky and Willinger compared the standard estimators
systematically in 1995 and found systematic biases and strong sensitivity to the estimation method
and to the range of scales used in the fit [@taqqu1995]. Dimensions estimated by box-counting and
by dividers on the same object do not agree in general, and both are sensitive to where the fit
starts and stops.

The practical consequence is easy to state. The claim "this object is rough in a scale-invariant
way" is fairly robust. The claim "its dimension is 1.32" is not, and the second claim is the one
that gets quoted.

There is also a purely arithmetic requirement that is routinely ignored. A power law can only be
observed over the range of scales the data covers, and over a short range almost any smooth curve
is indistinguishable from a power law. If a series covers one order of magnitude, the fitted
exponent is largely a description of the fitting window, not of the object.

This is the point at which the book has to propose something rather than report something.

## Proposed: the scale-span rule

**The rule.** An exponent may be reported only together with the span of scales over which it was
fitted. A span smaller than two orders of magnitude shall not be reported as a property of the
object under study; it may be reported as a description of the data within that window.

**Why two orders.** The threshold is a convention, and I want to be clear that it is a convention
rather than a derived constant. It is chosen because a decade of scale is about the smallest range
over which the curvature of a plausible alternative model becomes detectable in a log-log plot.
Readers who prefer three decades have an argument; the rule's content is the reporting
requirement, not the number.

**How to test the rule.** Take a function that is known not to be scale-invariant — a parabola, a
sum of two exponentials, a logistic curve — sample it over one order of magnitude, and fit a power
law. If the fit is acceptable by the usual criteria, the span was too short to support an
exponent, whatever the object's true structure.

**Precondition.** The rule requires that the scale span be measurable, which excludes series whose
sampling resolution changes over time, and series whose units are not comparable across the
sample.

[N] The scale-span rule is proposed by this book and registered as entry B-008 in
`verify/constructed.csv`. The two-orders threshold is a convention chosen for reporting, not a
result.

## The scale-span rule applied to three studies

The rule proposed in the previous section is easy to state and easy to forget. Here is what it does
when applied to three pieces of published work cited in this chapter.

**Taqqu, Teverovsky and Willinger (1995).** The purpose of the study was methodological, and its
conclusion — that estimators disagree and are sensitive to the fitting range — is itself an
argument for reporting the range. The paper's contribution survives the rule; indeed the rule is
close to a normative restatement of its findings.

**Box-counting studies in the biological literature.** These typically work with image resolutions
spanning one to two orders of magnitude. Under the rule, their exponents are descriptions of the
images at the available resolutions and should be reported as such, not as properties of the
organisms. The substantive biological conclusions often survive this reframing; the numerical
precision claims do not.

**Coastline studies.** Modern re-measurements of specific coastlines work with map or satellite
data covering two to three orders of magnitude, and they can clear the threshold. Their difficulty
is a different one: the object itself is not scale-invariant over the whole range, because a
continent's outline is influenced by tectonic structure at the largest scales.

Notice the pattern. The rule does not tell you a study is wrong. It tells you which sentence in the
study is licensed by the data and which is not, and the sentence that is not licensed is usually
the one that appears in the abstract.

## The scale-span rule as a checklist

Because the rule is a convention rather than a theorem, its value is in being applied. Five steps,
worth running on any exponent you meet, including the ones in this book.

**One. Find the span.** What range of scales does the data cover? If the paper does not say, the
paper has not reported the exponent, whatever else it reports.

**Two. Convert the span into decades.** Ratios, not differences: a series running from one second to
one hour spans about three and a half decades.

**Three. Check the fit's shape.** On a log-log plot, is the relationship straight over the whole
span, or straight over part of it? A break in the line means two regimes, and an exponent fitted
across a break is a description of neither.

**Four. Ask what else fits.** A power law and a stretched exponential look similar over two
decades. If the conclusion depends on which one is true, the span is too short to carry the
conclusion.

**Five. Write the exponent with its window.** "The exponent is 1.6 over the range from one minute to
one day" is a finding. "The exponent is 1.6" is a rumour.

The checklist takes ten minutes and it has never failed to change my reading of a paper. Sometimes
it changes the reading in the paper's favour, which is the outcome I did not expect the first few
times it happened.

## What the paper concedes

The paper's limits are stated by its author, in the text, and they are more candid than most of its
readers assume. Three passages are worth quoting, because they set the boundary of everything
above.

On the mathematics: the conditions under which a similarity dimension exists are, in the paper's
words, not a fully solved problem. On the strength of the inference: the most that can be said
with perfect safety is that the observed regularity is *compatible* with the idea that
geographical curves are random self-similar figures of fractional dimension. And on the state of
the field, in a footnote: the concept of dimension is elusive and very complex, and the field
abounds in paradoxes.

So the paper's own claim is a compatibility claim. That is, it argues that the data are consistent
with a certain structure, and it does not claim to have proved that the structure holds.

I take this as the model for how to write a paper that will survive. The author had an
interpretation he believed, and he told the reader exactly how much of it the evidence supported.

## Claim and tool

**The claim** was that natural coastlines are statistically self-similar, with a fractional
dimension that can be estimated from length measurements at different scales. The claim has held
up better than the one in Chapter 1, and its quantitative content has not: dimension estimates
from natural objects turn out to depend strongly on the estimation method and the fitting window.

**The tool** is the move from a quantity to its behaviour under a change of scale. When a
measurement depends on the instrument, stop treating the dependence as error and start treating
it as the measurement. That move left geography within a few years and turned up in materials
science, image analysis, physiology, and network traffic.

The tool is also where the book's own device becomes useful. The dimension is a **scale constant**
at best: it survives a change of resolution, within a stated span, and it does not survive a
change in the estimating procedure. Treating it as a property of the object — a Grade I claim with
no stated transformation — is the error the scale-span rule is meant to prevent.

## Boundary conditions

The result holds when the object is statistically self-similar over the span you measure, and when
the span is wide enough for a power law to be distinguishable from the alternatives.

It fails when the span is short, when the object has a characteristic scale — most engineered
objects, most biological structures above the cellular level — and when the estimation method is
chosen after looking at the answer.

It says nothing about magnitude or consequence. A dimension is a description of geometry, and a
coastline's dimension tells you nothing about whether the sea will rise.

And it does not license the inference people most want to draw from it. Roughness is not the same
as danger, and scale invariance is not the same as predictability.

## Dimension as a description, not a property

The coastline measurement is easy to read as a discovery about coastlines. It is more usefully read as
a demonstration about measurement, and the difference decides how the result should be used.

**What the measurement produces.** A number relating two quantities: the length obtained and the
ruler used to obtain it. The slope of that relationship, on a log-log plot, is an estimate of a
dimension, and it is a summary of the data-generating procedure as much as of the object.

**What the measurement depends on.** Three things, all of which the practitioner controls.

The **range of rulers**. A measurement spanning three orders of magnitude and one spanning one order
will disagree, and the shorter span is not a smaller version of the longer one; it is a different
estimate of a possibly different quantity.

The **method of measurement**. Walking a pair of dividers along a map, counting boxes on a grid, and
estimating a spectral slope are three procedures with three biases. Part I used them interchangeably
and obtained three different answers, which is why the book's figure for this chapter was produced by
a construction whose answer is known independently.

The **definition of the object**. A coastline's length depends on where the land ends, which is itself
a question about scale. At the scale of a molecule there is no coastline; at the scale of a continent
there is a different one.

**Why the number nevertheless travels.** Because comparisons between objects measured by the same
procedure are meaningful. Two river networks measured identically can be compared; one measured by
dividers and one by box-counting cannot. **The dimension is a relation, and the relation is only as
reliable as the invariance of the procedure.**

**The category error, stated plainly.** Saying that a coastline "has" a dimension of about one and a
quarter is like saying that a road "has" a travel time of forty minutes. The number is real and the
attribution is wrong: it belongs to the journey and the route, or in this case to the measurement and
its range. The book's claim is about what can be measured and compared, not about what objects
contain.

**What follows for practice.** State the procedure. State the range. Report more than one method
where the comparison matters. And treat a change in dimension across ranges as a finding rather than
as an error, because a boundary between two scaling regimes is often the most informative thing in
the data.

## The ruler and the question

The coastline problem is usually presented as a discovery about measurement error. It is better
presented as a discovery about the interaction between an instrument and a question.

**Three ways to measure a length.**

**Stepping. Slow and observable.** Walk a pair of dividers of fixed length along the curve and count
the steps. The count times the step length is the measurement. The procedure is transparent, and its
answer depends on where the dividers are placed, which introduces a variance that the other methods do
not have.

**Covering. Fast and robust.** Cover the curve with squares of a fixed size on a grid, count the
occupied squares, and multiply. No placement decisions are required, and the estimate is smoother. The
grid's orientation, however, is a choice.

**Spectral. Indirect.** Estimate how variance is distributed across frequencies and infer a scaling
exponent. This requires no geometric measurement at all, which is a strength and a source of
disagreement with the other two.

**Why the three give different answers.** Not because any of them is wrong. Each measures a slightly
different property of a curve that has finite thickness, and the descriptions coincide only in a limit
that real objects do not reach.

**What follows for practice.** Where a dimension is reported, the procedure belongs in the sentence. A
comparison between two objects measured identically is meaningful; a comparison between a stepping
estimate and a spectral estimate is a comparison between two questions.

**Why the paper was still right.** Because the disagreement between procedures, and its systematic
dependence on the ruler, is the finding. **A quantity whose value depends on the instrument is a
different kind of quantity, and noticing that was the contribution.**

## The measurement decision nobody records

The coastline exercise requires four decisions before any number is produced, and the record of a published
dimension rarely contains them.

**Decision one. What counts as the boundary.** A coastline's edge is a transition zone of finite width.
**Where the zone is drawn is a choice, and at the finest scales the choice determines the answer.**

**Decision two. What resolution the source data have.** A map at a given scale has already smoothed the
object. **Measuring below the map's resolution measures the cartography rather than the coast.**

**Decision three. Which method.** Stepping, covering and spectral estimation answer different questions.

**Decision four. What range to fit.** The boundary between the method's reliable range and its noise floor is
itself a judgement.

**What recording the four decisions costs.** Two sentences. **What omitting them costs: the dimension becomes
a property of the object rather than a result of a procedure, which is the category error the chapter
identifies.**

**The test for a reader.** Take a published dimension and ask which of the four decisions it implies. **Where
the paper does not say, the number cannot be reproduced even in principle, and irreproducibility is a
different problem from wrongness — it is the absence of a claim that could be checked at all.**

**Why this matters beyond geography.** Every scaling measurement in this book's material faces the same four
decisions: a tail index requires a cut-off, a memory parameter requires a bandwidth, a dimension requires a
ruler. **The decisions are the analysis, and the number is their residue.**

## The coastline as a template for a measurement dispute

The disagreement the paper provoked has a shape that recurs whenever a quantity turns out to depend on the
instrument, and the shape is worth extracting.

**The four moves of the dispute.**

**A measurement is reported.** A length, a dimension, a scaling exponent.

**A critic measures differently and reports a different number.** Both procedures are defensible. **The
disagreement is not about arithmetic.**

**The disagreement is resolved by identifying the procedure, not by reconciling the numbers.** The two results
stand, each indexed to its method. **Neither is withdrawn and neither is wrong.**

**The quantity is redefined to include the procedure.** What is reported becomes "the length measured this way
over this range". **The redefinition is the resolution, and it is a change in what the number means rather
than in what it is.**

**Where the same shape appears in this book. Three places.**

**Tail exponents.** Rank-based and likelihood estimators disagree, and the resolution is to report both with
their cut-offs.

**Memory parameters.** Estimators vary with bandwidth, and the resolution is the effective-sample correction.

**Cross-sectional correlations.** Correlations depend on the window, and the resolution is to report the
window.

**What the template predicts.** A quantity that cannot be reported without its procedure will be contested for
as long as the procedure is omitted. **The contest is not a sign that the field is confused; it is a sign that
the reporting convention has not yet absorbed the dependence.**

**Why the paper is worth reading for this reason alone.** Because it is a clean case of a measurement dispute
resolved correctly, and the resolution is available in four pages. **Most such disputes in this book's material
take decades, and the difference is that here the object was a coastline, which nobody had a position in.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The full text of Mandelbrot (1967) was not available to me. The argument above rests on the
abstract, the figure captions, the reference list, and the passages quoted in the secondary
literature; the six values and the paper's own descriptions of its selection criteria come from
sources that reproduce the paper's page 637 table, and I have flagged which of my statements are
interpretations rather than quotations.

The critiques of box-counting cited in the estimation section were located by record rather than
read in full, and their content is described here only at the level their titles and abstracts
support.

And the two-orders convention in the scale-span rule is mine. It is published in the constructed
register so that it can be argued with.
